title: Haggai
subtitle: the prophet who got a stalled Temple moving
lead: Haggai is the second-shortest book of the Prophets and the most exactly dated. Between 29 August and 18 December of 520 BC, a prophet in Jerusalem brings four dated messages to the governor Zerubbabel, the high priest Joshua and the people of the small Persian province of Judah. The Temple that Cyrus had allowed them to rebuild lay unfinished, and the people were saying that the time had not come. Haggai tells them to look at their lean harvests and their finished houses, and to go up into the hills for wood.

The leaders and the people listen, and the work starts 23 days later. The next messages answer the discouragement that follows: the new house looks like nothing beside Solomon's, the people's offerings are unclean until the house is built, and the LORD will shake the heavens, the earth and the nations. He promises that the last glory of this house will be greater than the first, and he ends with a word to Zerubbabel alone: "I will make you like a seal ring, for I have chosen you." The Temple was finished five years later, in March 515 BC (Ezra 6:15).
facts: The prophet Haggai is the speaker, but the book speaks of him in the third person, so it was put together by someone else, perhaps a disciple or a later editor. Jewish tradition says the Men of the Great Assembly wrote the Twelve (Bava Batra 15a).

The four dated messages are between 29 August and 18 December 520 BC by the usual conversion, in the second year of Darius I. The book was shaped soon after, or later in the Persian period; the scholarly debate is summarized under "Date, unity and sources."
Jerusalem and the province of Judah (Hebrew Yehud), part of the Persian Empire's region "Beyond the River", about 66 years after the first Temple was burned and 18 years after Cyrus's decree.

Prose, in dated reports of prophetic messages with short quoted speech: a rebuke and a call, a short report of the people's obedience, an encouragement, a ruling by the priests and a promise. It is not poetry, though the style rises into a more elevated, rhetorical voice at 2:6-9 and 2:21-23. The same formulas return: "Take your ways to heart" (1:5, 7; 2:15, 18), "the word of the LORD came through Haggai," and "the LORD declares."
Hebrew, in a plain prose style, with a few rare words such as mal'akut ("message," found only here) and the title governor (pechah).
2 chapters, 38 verses in English and Hebrew numbering (15, 23)

English and Hebrew agree throughout. The date of 1:15 closes chapter 1 in both. The Greek (Swete's text) places the sixth-month date at the start of chapter 2, so its chapter 1 has 14 verses; this site uses the English and Hebrew numbers.

The tenth of the Twelve Minor Prophets in both the Hebrew order (Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi) and the Greek order (Hosea, Amos, Micah, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai...). It is the first of the three post-exilic prophets, with Zechariah and Malachi.

History (H), Critical (C), Jewish tradition (J) and Christian (X) apply to the whole book. The Still-to-come lens (F) applies only to 2:6-9 and 2:21-23, where the shaking of the nations and the seal ring are read as still to come in some traditions.
authorship: Haggai the prophet spoke the messages, and he or a scribe put them in order. The Talmud counts him with Zechariah and Malachi among the last prophets, after whom the Holy Spirit left Israel (Yoma 9b), and says the Men of the Great Assembly wrote the Twelve (Bava Batra 15a).

The book is a compilation of Haggai's messages by an editor who writes about him in the third person ("Haggai the prophet," "the LORD's messenger"), dates each message in a fixed formula, and tells the response (1:12-15). The editor may have been a disciple soon after 520, or a later hand connected with the editing of Zechariah 1-8 (Ackroyd, Meyers and Meyers, Petersen, Wolff, Kessler). The shared dates and the shared formulas suggest that Haggai and Zechariah 1-8 were edited together at some stage (Redditt).

Some argue that the book stays close to Haggai's own speech and was recorded quickly, because its setting, dates and details agree with Ezra 5-6; others find the whole of it the work of Haggai's circle.

audience.to: The first hearers were the two leaders of the small Judean community, Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest, and the people of Judah who had returned from Babylon or stayed in the land: a small, poor farming province under the Persian Empire, in a year when the new king Darius was still putting down revolts. The book's first readers, if it was edited later, were Judeans of the Persian period who knew the finished Temple and needed to know how it was begun.
audience.why: To get a stalled building going again, and to keep it going. The first message answers an excuse ("the time has not come") with an inventory of what the people were really doing and what was happening to their harvests. The next messages answer the discouragement, the doubt about holiness, and the fear of the powers around them. Knowing the audience changes the reading: the book is not a rule that giving brings wealth, and not a general call to church building programs. It is a word to a particular small community at a particular turning point, in the language of the covenant they knew.
views: A message for the Persian-period community
The most common view (Meyers and Meyers, Petersen, Kessler): the audience is the returned community in 520 BC, and the book was shaped soon after to record how the Temple began.
Some see the book as written or edited for a later generation (the Chronicler's time, or after the Temple was completed) that had to understand why the Second Temple lacked the first's glory.
Read in the synagogue and the church

Both Jewish and Christian readers have heard the book as addressed to their own communities: the Jewish reading connects the Second Temple's lack of glory to the Temple's end, the Christian reading connects the temple to the church (1 Corinthians 3:16; 1 Peter 2:5).

outline: The call to build: "Take your ways to heart"
The leaders and the remnant obey, and the work begins
"Be strong": the first glory and the last
A ruling on holy and unclean, and the promise "from this day I will bless"
The word to Zerubbabel: a seal ring

lenses.name: History
lenses.desc: Reads the book against the Persian period: Darius I in 520 BC, the province of Yehud, Zerubbabel and Joshua, the stalled Temple of Ezra 4-6, the failed harvests, and the completion in 515 BC. It asks what the dated messages can tell us and what the sources leave unsaid, such as what became of Zerubbabel.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the book was made and put in order, how it relates to Ezra 5-6 and to Zechariah 1-8, who "this people" are in 2:14, what "the day the foundation was laid" means, and which textual differences (the Greek additions at 2:9 and 2:14, the plural-or-singular question at 2:7) matter.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: Reads Haggai as Jews have read it: Rashi and Radak on the Temple and its promises, the Targum Jonathan at 2:7, the Talmud on the five things the Second Temple lacked and on the end of prophecy, and the discussion whether the Second Temple's glory was greater.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: Reads Haggai as the church has: the Vulgate's "Desired of all nations," Hebrews 12:26-27 on the shaking, the church as God's temple, Zerubbabel in the genealogies of Jesus (Matthew 1:12-13; Luke 3:27) and as a type of Christ, with the Fathers, Calvin and modern Catholic and Protestant commentators.

lenses.name: Still to come
lenses.desc: Used only for 2:6-9 and 2:21-23: readings that take the shaking of the heavens and the earth, the nations' wealth coming to a temple, and the seal-ring promise as events still ahead. Dispensationalist and some other readings join these verses to Ezekiel 40-48 and a millennial temple; others to the new creation.

sections.b:
Haggai is a book of dated speeches, and every speech answers an objection. Read it as a conversation between a prophet and a discouraged people: "The time has not come" (1:2) is answered by the empty barns (1:6-11); "It looks like nothing" (2:3) is answered by "I am with you" and the promise of glory (2:4-9); the doubt whether the people's work can be holy (2:10-14) is answered by the turn from this day (2:15-19); and the fear of the nations is answered by the seal ring (2:20-23).

The Plain keeps the book's repeated phrases the same English each time: "The LORD of Armies says this," "the LORD declares," "the word of the LORD came through Haggai," and above all "Take your ways to heart" (1:5, 7; 2:15, 18). The book speaks of Judah's leaders by their Persian-period titles: Zerubbabel is governor (pechah) and Joshua is the high priest, "the great priest." The same man is called Jeshua in Ezra and Nehemiah, and Joshua here, where the Hebrew has the longer name.

English and Hebrew verse numbers agree in Haggai: 38 verses, 15 in chapter 1 and 23 in chapter 2. The Greek (Swete's text) puts the sixth-month date of 1:15 at the start of chapter 2, as "the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month" before "the seventh month." This site uses the English and Hebrew numbers.

The base text is the Leningrad Codex. The Greek is read in Swete's edition, which prints mainly Codex Vaticanus; the critical editions (Rahlfs and Hanhart; the Göttingen Duodecim Prophetae) were not consulted. The Dead Sea Scroll transcriptions were read in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook data: 4Q77 (4QXIIb), 4Q80 (4QXIIe) and the Murabba'at scroll of the Twelve, Mur88. Mur88 preserves most of both chapters and agrees with the Masoretic Text in meaning wherever the transcription is not restored; its small differences are noted in the variants (for example "to Haggai" at 2:1). 4Q77 preserves only a few verses (1:1-2; 2:2-4) and 4Q80 a few later ones (2:18-21). The Greek Minor Prophets scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr) was not used. The notable differences are in the Greek: "of the tribe of Judah" for "governor" (1:1, 1:14, 2:2, 2:21, and added at 1:12), "sword" for "drought" (1:11), no clause about the covenant in 2:5, a plural "chosen things" in 2:7, a sentence about peace of soul in 2:9, a long addition in 2:14, and a different question in 2:19. The Latin Vulgate's "Desired of all nations" (2:7) is cited from the Clementine printing. The Targum and Peshitta are later and were not used as sources for the Plain.

The dates fix the messages in 520 BC. The first and last are four months apart, and the Temple was finished in 515 (Ezra 6:15). Most scholars think the book took its form in Haggai's circle, soon after, and that its editor also had a hand in Zechariah 1-8: both books date their messages by Darius's year, month and day, use similar formulas, and name the same two leaders. Ezra 5:1 and 6:14 give Haggai and Zechariah together the credit for the work, which supports a link. Many think the narrative frame (1:1, 3, 12-15; 2:1, 10, 20) is the editor's; others defend a closer link to Haggai himself. The passage 2:10-19 is the hardest to place; some think it is out of order, some that "this people" are the Samaritans (Rothstein, 1908), and most that it is Haggai's own message to the Judeans on the day the work reached a milestone.

Haggai opens a short series of dated post-exilic books: Haggai and Zechariah 1-8 are dated within a few months of each other (the second year of Darius), and Zechariah 7 is dated two years later. Malachi has no date. The Hebrew order of the Twelve puts Haggai after Zephaniah, which ends with a promise of restoration, and before Zechariah. Some modern readers (Nogalski, Redditt) see the Twelve edited as one scroll, with Haggai and Zechariah as a pair; that the Twelve were a single book is debated. The Jewish tradition says the Twelve were one scroll, written by the Men of the Great Assembly (Bava Batra 15a).

sections.h: How Jews and Christians have used the book
sections.b:
For Jewish readers Haggai is a prophet of the Second Temple, one of the last three. The Talmud draws on the missing letter in 1:8 for the five things the Second Temple lacked (Yoma 21b) and on the end of prophecy (Yoma 9b), and the debate whether the Second Temple's "last glory" was greater (2:9, reported by Rashi) became part of the Jewish memory of the Temple. The Targum of the Prophets is said to come from Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi (Megillah 3a). Sirach praises Zerubbabel and Joshua (Jeshua) in turn (Sirach 49:11-12).

For Christians, the shaking of the heavens and the earth is quoted in Hebrews 12:26-27, Zerubbabel appears in the genealogies of Jesus (Matthew 1:12-13; Luke 3:27), and the Latin "Desired of all nations" became a title of Christ in Advent worship. These uses are receptions of the book and are labeled so in the notes. The misuse of 1:6-11 as a promise of wealth for giving is a modern reading that the Hebrew does not support.

spec.title: Claude's theory: five answers to five objections
spec.body: My reading is that the five dated units are built, in order, as answers to the five things a discouraged builder could say. "The time has not come" (1:2) is answered by 1:4-11. "We cannot afford to" is answered by 1:13-15 (the LORD is with you) and 2:8 (the silver is mine). "It looks like nothing" (2:3) is answered by 2:4-9. The doubt that their work is not clean enough (2:12-14) is answered by 2:15-19. "The empire is too strong" is answered by the shaking and the seal ring (2:20-23). The book is arranged so that no objection is left unanswered, which would explain why its messages are short and the dates exact. This overlaps with commentators who outline the book by the community's situation and questions; the five-objection scheme is my own labeled framing.

prompts: A hand-drawn scroll picture, ink and earth colors, of men and women in rough Persian-period clothes climbing a stony hillside to cut timber, a half-built stone wall of a small temple in the background and a bare empty barn at one side. Cave-drawing figures, soft torn edges like old parchment, no hard rectangle.
The old men weeping at the foundation

A sketch on aged papyrus in a mix of ancient manuscript style and modern line art: old priests with white beards standing at a low new stone foundation, some weeping, some shouting, young builders behind them. Soft uneven borders, a few Hebrew letters in the margin.

A hand-drawn scroll illustration of a large hand with a carved seal ring pressing its mark into soft clay, a crown lying broken beside it and the shapes of toppled chariots and horses at the edges. Ink, ochre and indigo, edges faded like a worn scroll.
reading: Carol L. Meyers and Eric M. Meyers, Haggai, Zechariah 1-8 (Anchor Bible 25B, 1987)
The fullest commentary: the text, the Persian background, and archaeology, with the argument for the Temple as the center of the book.
David L. Petersen, Haggai and Zechariah 1-8 (Old Testament Library, 1984)
A clear historical commentary that reads Haggai and Zechariah together.
Hans Walter Wolff, Haggai: A Commentary (Augsburg, 1988)
A compact commentary on the text, structure and message, by a leading form critic.
John Kessler, The Book of Haggai: Prophecy and Society in Early Persian Yehud (2002)
A study of Haggai against the social and economic conditions of the province.
Peter R. Ackroyd, Exile and Restoration (1968)
The classic study of the exile and the post-exilic community, with long treatment of Haggai and Zechariah.
Mark J. Boda, Haggai, Zechariah (NIV Application Commentary, 2004)
An accessible commentary for readers who want both the history and the application.
